name: Cupping therapy

card.summary: A traditional suction-cup practice that people use for muscle tension and recovery and, in facial form, for skin glow and a de-puffed look.
card.note: Leaves circular bruise-like marks; burns and infection are reported with fire and wet cupping.

quick.overview:
Cupping places cups on the skin and creates suction, using heat or a hand pump, to draw tissue up into the cup. Practitioners use it for muscle tightness and recovery, and variants of cup massage are applied on the face for a brighter, less puffy look.

The appearance link is mostly indirect: easing tight muscles can support training and posture, and facial cupping is promoted for circulation and glow. Research has focused on pain, where reviews report benefits for conditions such as low back pain, while one sham-controlled trial found dry cupping no better than sham.
quick.how: Dry cupping uses suction alone, fire cupping uses a flame to create the vacuum, and wet (hijama) cupping draws a small amount of blood. Sessions are commonly given on the back, and cups may be moved over oiled skin. Marks fade over days to weeks.
quick.risks: Marks, bruising, burns (with fire cupping), infection (with wet cupping), scarring and skin discoloration are reported. It is not suitable for everyone, and health authorities in Cambodia have warned people with high blood pressure or heart problems.

lead: Cupping therapy places cups on the skin and creates suction, either by warming the air inside the cup or with a hand pump, so that skin and underlying tissue are drawn up into the cup.[1][2] It is practised mainly in Asia and also in Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Latin America, and it appears in traditional Chinese, Islamic (hijama), Greek and Roman medicine.[1][5]

People use cupping to ease muscle tightness, soreness and back or neck pain and to support recovery between training sessions, which is the chain by which it connects to a better-looking physique: less tension, more comfortable training, better posture and movement.[1][6] Practitioners of traditional Chinese medicine describe it as dispelling stagnation and improving the flow of qi, and a cosmetic offshoot, facial cupping with small soft cups moved over oiled skin, is promoted for circulation, a flushed glow and a de-puffed look.[1] Cupping also leaves round, bruise-like marks that last days to weeks; they are the visible signature of the technique and are sometimes worn openly.[1][9]

Athletes brought the marks to wide attention, most notably Michael Phelps at the 2016 Rio Olympics, and others cited by Wikipedia include Shaquille O'Neal, DeMarcus Ware, Natalie Coughlin, Alex Naddour and Ben Shelton.[1] Wikipedia classes cupping as pseudoscience and notes that critics have called it quackery, while systematic reviews report possible benefit for some pain conditions and caution that effects may not differ from placebo.[1][3][5][7] The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says most cupping research is of low quality.[9]

chain: Suction draws blood to the skin and loosens muscle
Looser feeling, brighter or de-puffed look claimed
angle.text: Proponents use cupping to relax muscles and to give the face a flushed, lifted look. The skin and facial effects are claimed rather than measured, and the marks themselves are visible for some time.

paras: Wikipedia distinguishes several forms.[1] In dry cupping a heated cup is placed on the back, chest, abdomen or buttocks and suction develops as the air cools; modern versions use plastic or silicone cups and a manual pump or electric device instead of flame.[1][10] In fire cupping, a cotton ball soaked in alcohol is lit, briefly placed in the cup, removed, and the cup set on the skin.[1] Oil may be applied so that cups can glide over muscle groups in sliding or massage cupping.[1] In wet cupping, called hijama in Arabic, blood is drawn by suction after the skin is lightly incised.[1] Sessions typically last 5 to 15 minutes per placement, and cups have historically been made of glass, bamboo, horn, copper and bronze.[1]
A 2018 overview proposed new ways to classify cupping by technique, suction strength and the materials used with it, noting that cupping is often combined with acupuncture.[2][1]

Facial cupping adapts the technique with small, soft cups that are lightly moved over oiled facial skin. Proponents promote it for a rosy glow, a lifted look and less puffiness.[1] The skin and facial effects are claimed rather than measured: no trials of cupping for facial appearance were found, and Wikipedia states that evidence for acne is lacking.[1] The marks from stronger body cupping are visible for some time, which is one reason practitioners distinguish gentler gliding techniques.[1]

Wikipedia reports that Hippocrates reportedly used cupping for internal disease and that Roman surgeons used it for bloodletting; wet cupping appears in Iranian traditional medicine, and Islamic medical scholars developed the method further.[1] A narrative review of hijama notes that the exact origin is debated but that use is documented in early Egyptian and Chinese medical practice.[4] The earliest recorded Chinese use is attributed to Ge Hong (281-341 AD), and Chinese hospitals have used cupping since the 1950s.[1]

Wikipedia adds that Maimonides mentioned it, that it was practised in Eastern European Jewish communities, that a sauna-based horn-cup form has been practised in Finland since the 15th century, and that William Osler recommended it for pneumonia in the early 20th century.[1] George Orwell described cupping in his 1946 essay How the Poor Die, and it appears in the 1964 film Zorba the Greek.[1]

Traditional Chinese medicine explains cupping as dispelling stagnation and improving the flow of qi, often over acupuncture points.[1] Practitioners also say it removes toxins or stagnant blood and improves circulation.[1] Modern reviews offer other candidate mechanisms: the pain-gate theory, in which suction stimulates nerve fibres and dampens pain signals, and local release of nitric oxide that may improve circulation and muscle relaxation; the authors of one review note that the mechanism of action is not fully understood.[10][3] Critics cited on Wikipedia, including Harriet Hall, Mark Crislip, David Colquhoun and David Gorski, reject the detoxification and blood-flow explanations as implausible, noting that a cupping bruise is a pooled clot rather than flowing blood.[1]
Human research has concentrated on pain and musculoskeletal conditions, with much of it from China, Korea and the Middle East.

An evidence map of 13 systematic reviews (searched to March 2021) found that six reported potential benefit in conditions including low back pain, ankylosing spondylitis, knee osteoarthritis, neck pain, herpes zoster, migraine, plaque psoriasis and chronic urticaria.[5] A 2024 meta-analysis of 11 trials with 921 participants reported that cupping improved low back pain at two to eight weeks.[7] A 2023 review of 22 randomised and case-series studies of musculoskeletal and sports conditions found that most trials used dry cupping and concluded that the evidence base was still developing.[6]

Wikipedia reports that a 2011 review found effectiveness poorly documented for most conditions and a 2014 review attributed earlier positive findings to weak study design, and that later reviews cite inconsistent blinding and varied methods; it describes evidence for musculoskeletal and myofascial pain as low to moderate and possibly no different from placebo.[1] The American Cancer Society states that the evidence does not support health benefits.[1]

A randomised trial with 90 participants and concealed allocation found dry cupping not superior to sham cupping for chronic non-specific low back pain.[8] More recent randomised trials have examined wet cupping and acupuncture for migraine,[11] wet cupping in fibromyalgia,[12] dry cupping added to core-stabilisation exercise for sacroiliac joint dysfunction,[13] and acupuncture plus wet cupping for post-stroke depression in 130 patients.[14] No trials of cupping for facial appearance or skin quality were found.

Wikipedia reports that cupping is generally considered safe for most people when performed by trained practitioners but may not suit everyone, and that traditional practice avoids cupping over skin ulcers and, in TCM, over the abdomen or sacral area of pregnant women.[1] NCCIH lists persistent skin discoloration, scars, burns, infections and worsening of eczema or psoriasis as possible side effects, and describes rare severe cases including bleeding inside the skull after scalp cupping and anaemia from repeated wet cupping; shared, unsterilised equipment can spread bloodborne infections such as hepatitis B and C.[9] Burns are documented with fire cupping.[1]

Because the marks resemble injuries, NCCIH advises telling healthcare providers where they came from, and Wikipedia notes that cupping bruises have been mistaken for signs of child abuse, in rare cases leading to legal action against parents.[1][9] Cambodia's health ministry warned in 2016 that cupping could be dangerous for people with high blood pressure or heart problems.[1]

Phelps's circular marks at the 2016 Olympics drew worldwide media attention, and Wikipedia lists a series of other athletes who have used it.[1] Critics including Brad McKay and Steven Novella have condemned the promotion of cupping in elite sport, and Wikipedia notes that celebrity endorsement may lead people to perceive benefits that are not objectively present.[1] Supporters in sport describe it as a recovery tool; the 2023 sports-rehabilitation review notes that athletes' use has prompted research interest.[6]

lore.intro: Cupping is discussed in looksmaxxing and wellness circles mainly as a recovery and tension-release tool, and in beauty media as facial cupping; the claims below are those made by practitioners and promoters.[1]

claims.claim: Cupping removes toxins and stagnant blood.
claims.believers: Traditional and TCM practitioners say suction draws out toxins, stagnation or vital energy.[1]
claims.experts: Critics cited on Wikipedia say a cupping bruise is a blood clot, not flowing blood, and describe detoxification claims as unsupported.[1]

claims.claim: Cupping improves circulation and muscle relaxation.
claims.believers: Proponents describe local vasodilation and relaxed muscle after sessions.[1]
claims.experts: Reviews propose nitric oxide release and pain-gate effects as possible mechanisms but state that the mechanism is not fully understood.[3][10]

claims.claim: Cupping relieves back and neck pain.
claims.believers: Users and practitioners report easier movement and less soreness after sessions.[1]
claims.experts: A 2024 meta-analysis of 11 trials reported improved low back pain at 2-8 weeks, while a sham-controlled trial of 90 people found dry cupping not superior to sham.[7][8]

claims.believers: Athletes including Michael Phelps have used it and popularised it.[1]
claims.experts: A 2023 review of 22 musculoskeletal and sports studies concluded that the evidence base is still limited.[6]

claims.claim: Facial cupping gives a glow and reduces puffiness.
claims.believers: Promoters say gentle suction on the face boosts circulation, giving a flushed, lifted look.[1]
claims.experts: No trials of facial cupping were found, and Wikipedia states that evidence for acne is lacking.[1]

claims.claim: Cupping marks are harmless and fade quickly.
claims.believers: Practitioners say marks are painless and fade over days to weeks.[1]
claims.experts: NCCIH lists persistent discoloration, scars, burns and infections as possible effects and notes that marks can be mistaken for abuse.[9]
